utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As all can see, Mr. Milutinovic's counsel are not present this morning. The Trial Chamber has been given certain information, it may be that there are others here who can supplement that information, I don't know, but Mr. O'Sullivan I gather is unwell and Mr. Zecevic on his way back from Belgrade. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information I have, I've been in communication with Mr. O'Sullivan by e-mail, the flight that Mr. Zecevic is on is scheduled to land at 10.30 but rarely does so. It's a flight out of Belgrade on JAT. You can't be certain when they might arrive but they try to arrive at 10.30. So I don't know quite how you want to deal with the possibility that Mr. Zecevic could be here by noon perhaps if everything works well. That's probably the best I can give you right now. Maybe there's a possibility I don't know of rescheduling for an afternoon schedule. That would solve all the problems, but I don't know if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not possible at the moment because I don't have enough information about the plans for the other cases. The programme on the face of it is a full one today, apart from court 2 this morning and this doesn't assist with the resolution of this difficulty. It's -- unless there was a particular suggestion from the Defence to proceed in their absence, it's not our view that that should happen. Even though there are clearly electronic facilities available which could assist, but we're not inclined to abandon the day completely at this stage. So I intend to -- can you tell me, just before I go further, Mr. Ackerman, how does Mr. Zecevic normally get from the airport to here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think he normally comes by taxi, which would be the fastest way to get here. I think that's what he normally uses so he would get here as -- I think he's aware of the situation so he would try to get here as quickly as possible. And I might say that it's remarkable that we've gone this far without an illness interrupting our proceedings. That's unprecedented at the Tribunal, certainly in my experience here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree, but the experience of the end of the Prosecution case tells us that what we ought to do is have time in the bank, if we can, for later. So it's obviously possible that we could sit from 12.00 to 1.45, which we consider would be worth doing. If then there was a facility for proceeding further, we could do that as well, but at the moment there's no immediate prospect of that. There's probably no good reason for trying to sit any earlier than 12.00 because if we're stuck with the morning only we would gain no more time by making it 11.30 than 12.00 because of translation. The only way it would be worth sitting earlier if very soon it became known that one of the other cases was not going to sit this afternoon. So what I suggest is that you stay around for half an hour while inquiries are made, but unless something opens up immediately then we'll stand down until 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a suggestion. We will know by 10.30, 10.45 whether that flight is actually in and whether Mr. Zecevic will actually be able to be here within the time of the morning sitting. And what I suggest is that we wait that half-hour that you just suggested. And if there's no resolution at that point, that we assume there will be no more hearing this afternoon unless we hear different by e-mail so that we can leave here and actually get some meaningful work done. I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand your point of view, Mr. Ackerman, we always bear it in mind. But let's see what emerges in the next half-hour, and the clerk will then convey the situation to you. But for the moment we shall anticipate sitting at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gajic -- or, in fact, good afternoon now. Sorry about the hold-up --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- But an unexpected illness has caused the hold-up this morning and this is the earliest that we could continue with the proceedings. I hope that you do not suffer too much inconvenience as a result. Your examination by Mr. Visnjic will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, on Friday as the session drew to a close we spoke about the briefing that General Farkas had at the collegium meeting of the 8th of June, 1999, and tasks that the Chief of General Staff, or rather, at that time chief of the Supreme Command Staff issued after that meeting. Could you please tell me whether this activity, the conducting of investigations into violations of humanitarian law, or rather, war crimes, continued after the hostilities ceased in June 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like 3D1056 to be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in front of us we see a document dated the 21st of June, 1999, and among other addressees there is your name. Could you please tell us what is this document about, briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this concerns a military conscript Stevan Jekic, as can be seen from this document. A criminal report was filed against him by the military police of the 37th Motorised Brigade from Raska because of --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, we can see that from the document. We can see the crimes here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit 3D1057.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document dated the 25th of June, 1999. Could you please tell me briefly again what this document is all about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is about Rados Avramovic from the same unit as Jekic, that is the 37thth Motorised Brigade, a criminal report was filed against him, too, and I think that it was filed for the same criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to be shown Defence Exhibit 3D1058.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, that's a document dated the 25th of June, 1999. Could you please tell us something about this case.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're now talking about four conscripts from the 37th Motorised Brigade and criminal reports were filed against them. And as you can see, they were in the military remand prison because of criminal offences that are violations of the international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit 3D1059.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell me something about the contents of this document. It's again one of the reports, it's an addendum, amendment to the report made after the end of the combat operations, the 25th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the criminal offence of war crime, homicide, committed against two ethnic Albanians who were killed; and it is apparent that three volunteers were charged or criminal reports were filed against them. And a certain number of witnesses from this unit were interrogated, and that is the 23rd Infantry Brigade, or rather, the 252nd Armoured Brigade and the security department of the 3rd Army command informs the Supreme Command Staff that they would be remanded in the custody of the civilian court or they would be placed under the jurisdiction of the civilian court because they no longer were in the army, they were no longer in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What problems did you encounter, General, or were there any problems that you encountered when you investigated those incidents after the end of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had difficulties that all boiled down to the fact that after the end of the combat operations all those people who had been mobilised when the state of war had been declared were now demobilised, and they were civilians, ordinary citizens. The problem was locating them, some of them, knowing the nature of their crimes. They hid. Jekic, for instance, we arrested him on the 21st of June, and from the security department of the 3rd Army command we received a document on the 21st of June, and we immediately took him to the Nis investigation prison for further processing. So this was the main problem: Finding those people. A number of measures and activities had to be taken in operational terms, police activities, to locate those people. Some of them fled abroad. They took the opportunity because of the situation, so that was the main problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Defence Exhibit 3D1061.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this time this is a document from July, the 14th of July, 1999. Could you please tell us briefly what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a crime committed in the village of Mali Alos, Lipljan municipality, where 20 Albanian ethnic civilians were killed. The suspects were a group of volunteers from the 252nd Tactical Group. A criminal report was filed, and as far as I can remember there were 12 of those volunteers. A criminal report was filed, and they were arrested. An investigation was conducted, and here to the right you can see, since this is the 3rd Army command security department, I received this report from them personally, and here's my comment on the right-hand side, or rather, my views that were then put into a memo sent to Colonel Antic, who was the chief of the security department in the 3rd Army command, where I in essence demanded that this case be treated with utmost seriousness because this was a war crime, a major war crime, where 20 civilians were killed, that this should be coordinated with the investigating judge, that they should also get in touch with the 1st Army because some of these people were from the 1st Army, conscripts, and that there should be more coordination with the military investigative organs, the court, and so on. As far as I know, this case was brought to a close. And just to make a brief note because I spoke on Friday about the meeting between the chief of the Supreme Command Staff of the 16th of May, General Pavkovic brought up this case at the meeting. And on the 17th in meeting with President Milosevic, he personally ordered that this case be treated with utmost seriousness, that all the perpetrators have to be prosecuted and punished. As far as I know, sometime in the year 2000 the military court threw this criminal report off because in the investigation it was determined that patrol from the 252 Tactical Group had come under attack at the entrance to the village by a group of terrorists. And after two hours of fighting, these people were killed. They were killed as a consequence of this fighting. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at Defence Exhibit 3D1062.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a memo dated the 3rd of August, 1999. It's from the security administration of the Yugoslav Army General Staff. Could you please tell us -- could you please tell us briefly what this memo is all about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is along the lines of what you asked me at the beginning, whether the investigations continued, the investigations into war crimes pursuant to the order of the Supreme Command Staff -- chief of Supreme Command Staff, that this should be vigorously prosecuted and that all perpetrators must be prosecuted, brought to justice, and punished. This is a memo where we ordered the security department of the 3rd Army command to improve the efficiency and to speed up the proceedings. We ordered them to set up an operational team of mixed composition. What does that mean? Operatives from the counter-intelligence service should be part of that team and also specialists from the military police units, forensic technicians, and so on. And that each and every case should be dealt with in a serious manner, that a plan should be done to investigate those cases, to compile criminal technical file, to submit everything to the criminal -- to the military prosecutor's office for further work. The security department is further ordered to get in touch with the security department in the 1st Army command, because some of the units from the 1st command were also deployed in Kosovo fighting the terrorist forces, and some of the persons who committed offences against the international humanitarian law were, in fact, in the area of responsibility of the 1st Army. And finally, it is ordered that the security administration should be kept informed so that we could monitor and guide their work and report to the Chief of the General Staff, or rather, Supreme Command Staff as he was styled at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit 3D1003.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, on Friday Judge Bonomy asked you to clarify who and how had to prosecute certain crimes. Now I'm waiting for this exhibit, 3D1003 to appear on our screens. General, this is a memo from the supreme military prosecutor dated the 11th of August, 1988, dealing with the jurisdiction of the courts over crimes against humanity and international law. Could you tell us very briefly whether this memo actually describes how you, the security administration, filed those criminal reports and to whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as you can see here right at the start, we asked the supreme military prosecutor for the clarifications in a document originating from us. And he provided us a detailed answer, and I think that the contents actually speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like you to go through this document. I would not like to do it now with the witness, but I do believe that it lays out in detail all the options at the disposal in prosecuting criminal offences at issue. And just very briefly, my colleague Mr. Sepenuk has just drawn my attention, there seems to be a problem with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me the year of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you please move it a little bit -- well, it's 1999, the 9th of August, so that was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that there is a mistake here on this document, it says in the upper left-hand corner 11th of August, 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there -- is that on the original or only on the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the original there is a stamp, a date stamp, so it's possible that the translator who produced the written translation couldn't actually see the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, Svetomir Obrencevic was not the supreme military prosecutor in 1988 if there are any doubts as to the exact date of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, on Friday we discussed the Pauk group. Again, it had to do with the subject raised by Judge Bonomy. In your statement in paragraph 156 you speak about Jugoslav Petrusic and Slobodan Orasanin. In order to clarify the matter to the Trial Chamber can you explain to us what the link is between the group Pauk and these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, this is a group of 23 persons altogether, whose leader, so to speak, was Jugoslav Petrusic. First there were grounds for suspicion and later on it was established that he was an agent of French intelligence from 1986. Orasanin was with him in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, again in paragraph 156 of your statement you speak of this person, Petrusic, and you link him to a number of killings and other crimes. What you are talking about -- rather, let me put it this way. When did these persons commit the crimes that you referred to in paragraph 156?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jugoslav Petrusic committed those crimes before he came to Yugoslavia, or rather, before he stayed with his group of 23 individuals in Kosovo and Metohija; that is to say that he did this while he worked for the French intelligence service, and these crimes were committed predominantly against individuals professing the Islamic faith because he was geared towards the Islamic factor in Africa primarily, but in some European countries, too. When there were interviews with him between the 18th of May and the 22nd of May, roughly, that is what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, that is what he stated during the investigation after he had been arrested, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Right. Tell me how was it that this group was discovered?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we in the security administration had some information about Mr. Petrusic being in contact with the French intelligence service, and then on the 8th of May, we called in for an interview of the security administration Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic, who was assistant for counter-intelligence in the department for security of the Pristina Corps. We asked him about that group. He said that this group was in Kosovo, that it was within the 125th Brigade, and that they had gone there, sidestepping the regular procedure that was based only the order issued by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command in terms of receiving volunteers and sending them to the theatre of war. And Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic said that they had some suspicions regarding his behaviour, especially the behaviour of Jugoslav Petrusic, but that they did not have any information about him, he -- or rather, and the members of his group having committed anything that was in contravention of international humanitarian law. This was later on confirmed because we did carry out an investigation. He also said that the suspicions they had and the information they had were presented to the command of the 125th Brigade, within which they were, and to the command of the Pristina Corps and that they were planning to remove them from Kosovo, which indeed happened soon after that. At the meeting with the then-President Milosevic on the 17th of May, General Vasiljevic spoke about that group, too. He said that we had suspicions to the effect that these were foreign agents, especially Petrusic, and General Pavkovic confirmed that, although he said then - and it was true - that there was no specific information confirming that they had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me further with this and explain what you mean by sidestepping the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for putting this question. I think that on Friday I explained that the order of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command dated the 16th of April regulated in detail the reception, recording, processing, and sending of volunteers to Kosovo and Metohija. Three reception centres were established: One was in Grocka near Belgrade, another in the village of Medja near Nis and yet the other one in the zone of the 2nd Army, that is to say Podgorica. That is to say all volunteers who volunteered would first of all have to go through the military district. The military district is a military territorial command. And then they are sent to a reception centre where they are recorded. Also, that is where they are processed from a health and security point of view. That is where they are made aware of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and international laws of war, and that is where they are told that they have to sign a statement that they would behave in accordance with these provisions and in accordance with the regulations of the Army of Yugoslavia. And that from that moment, when they sign that statement, they become members of the Army of Yugoslavia with the same status like any member who is doing his regular military service. As for this procedure regarding the group of Jugoslav Petrusic, this procedure was not carried through. Through some other channels we dealt with this through our own intelligence, not to bore you with all the details. They simply sidestepped this and that is why they came to Kosovo; however, we managed to recover them and return them in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you are asked by the interpreter to speak more slowly. I would like you to explain to me how they sidestepped the procedure. I understand there is a formal procedure. But you described their entry as sidestepping it. What does that mean? How did they become accepted in one of your official army brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well - how should I put this? - they had -- can I say that they had accomplices, if I can use that word. There were officers, individuals, some civilians, too, and quite simply they got through and they got down there. In a way, these persons provided guarantees for them and it happened. Mistakes are possible but they were quickly discovered and efficient measures were taken. Over there they were under control, so they didn't cause any damage. I'm trying to say that they did not commit a single crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a quite separate matter. Is it really that you don't know how this happened? I mean, nothing you've said so far is an explanation for them being accepted into a brigade of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were accepted through these people, these individuals who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Colonel Stupar was one of them. He's retired. I don't know whether he's alive. He used to serve in Kosovo, and he was one of the intermediaries who in a way provided guarantees for them and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there were some civilian persons, too. As for Orasanin, in view of the fact that he was involved in business, he had some connections in the military and probably, on the basis of what we managed to investigate and established, they mediated that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are these people, the colonel that you mentioned, Stupar, was he a colonel in the 125th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, but he served in Kosovo and he knew the situation there. He knew what the situation was like there. From earlier on he had these connections with Petrusic and Orasanin and so on and so forth. We clarified all of that, and I think that certain measures were taken against him too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but what I'm trying to understand is how they became accepted in the 125th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were accepted as volunteers; that is to say, these persons provided guarantees that they had gone through the procedure. But when we checked this, it was established that they had not gone through the procedure, whereas he had provided guarantees and he probably had certain connections in this reception centre, too. I'm not aware of all the details now, but we investigated this in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does that mean there was a system whereby anybody who had a position in the army could guarantee that the volunteers had come through the process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an omission and mistake that may happen, these things do happen. We quickly noticed this, the command and the counter-intelligence service, and efficient measures were taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've said that several times, Mr. Gajic. I'm just trying to understand how it happened in the first place. On Friday at around the same time as you were dealing with this matter, I tried to clarify with you what you meant by "paramilitary." Could you help me again with that. What did you mean when you referred to a "paramilitary"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means everything that is outside the prescribed system and legal regulations in relation to the reception of volunteers, and that is regulated in the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia. Those who wear uniform, either military or police uniforms, so that is illegal and that is paramilitary. That is to say that no one can be admitted into the army without this being done in accordance with the law specifically prescribed legal provisions in the Law on Defence and in the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What uniforms did the Pauk group wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, they were wearing some camouflage uniforms of their own, but they were not wearing uniforms of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you describe them as paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had gone through some procedure, but they did not go through the kind of procedure that they should have gone through. They had gone through some procedure, that is, they did not evade all proceedings, but it was not done as prescribed. They managed to avoid some things in relation to these connections of theirs and these channels. This, indeed, was an omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware of people in Serbia purchasing uniforms, using Deutschemarks to purchase uniforms, so that they could become involved in the action in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a broad-based question now. It was one of the problems, the fact that it was easy for anyone to get a uniform for a couple of hundred Deutschemarks, no problem about that. There were quite a few who came from Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska with uniforms, they even wore them, because people were poor and apart from those military uniforms, camouflage uniforms, they didn't have any other clothes, so it was no problem to obtain one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you to look at 3D1064. This is also a document containing information that was sent further on. Can you tell us briefly what the subject of this document is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document that was written on the basis of an order issued by the Chief of General Staff, and it pertains to obtaining information, documentation, et cetera, about crimes that were committed, as far as I ask see, by terrorist forces, the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, we've exhausted the subject by now. Just a few more questions, or rather, can you look at 4D135, please. General, we have a document here dated the 6th of June, 1999, and it says: Analysis of the implementation of the requests of the 3rd Army sent to the Supreme Command Staff. What's all of this about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an analysis on the implementation of the requests of the 3rd Army addressed to the Supreme Command Staff. As for the security administration, I think there should be some information here in terms of what was not carried through and why. It had to contain information as to why. And here it is, four tasks that were not carried out by the security administration, 25 per cent as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the B/C/S version in page -- page 3 and page 4 of the B/C/S version, and page 4 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, here it is, 2.4?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is stated there what was supposed to be resolved by the security administration and what was resolved out of what the 3rd Army had requested. Does this correspond to what you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond to what I remember, and it has to do with unimplemented tasks in relation to equipping military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, just some short documents. 3D589 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you're now -- your examination now has exceeded six hours in this case, that's well over the estimate, over 50 per cent more than the estimate. I just alert you to that. It looks as though we're going to have to address with you the whole question of timing. You're even over the piece exceeding your original estimate which preceded the number of hours available to the Defence to present their case. So I think you've got some hard thinking to do with how you're dealing with this. A lot of the evidence this morning could have been dealt with in writing. That's more or less what you're doing is asking someone to confirm the document that sets out the information. And now you're referring to another batch of documents, having on Friday told us that you would be able to do the rest of your examination in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have already taken some measures to cut my examination of my further witnesses short in order to make up for the time that I lost by examining Witness Gajic, but I have two more documents to go through and then I will be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's okay, Mr. Visnjic, but bear in mind that the total number of hours that the Defence indicated all the cases would take, of that we've allocated about 40 per cent at the time, the total time, available for the Defence. So adding two hours to one witness and knocking one and a half hours off by taking two names off the list simply means that your time's got longer. It's a much more radical approach that is necessary. There are ways of presenting large volumes of material here without doing it in realtime, in court, which is unrealistic. Anyway, let's try to get to the end of this examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please comment, or rather, explain to us under paragraph 2 on page 1 of the document, this is a briefing to the Chief of General Staff of the 18th of April, 1999, some information presented by the security administration is mentioned here and this information concerns the former verification mission in Kosovo. Could you please tell us what is this all about and where did you get this information, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is operative data that we obtained, indicating that in the work of agents in Kosovo, and these agents were put in place -- this agent network was put in place when the Kosovo Verification Mission was in Kosovo, but the infrastructure remained even after it pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any more exhibits to go through but I have three more questions. General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that, what's the mention -- the reference at the end of that paragraph to the drastic case regarding rape and looting in the Djakovica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a case of three soldiers who on the 16th of April, 1999, raped an underage Albanian girl, she was 16. This rape case -- this rape was reported by her father. The soldiers were identified, arrested, a criminal report was filed, and as far as I know they were convicted. They received prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you attended a number of meetings, including the meetings that were chaired by General Ojdanic at the command post in the Supreme Command Staff. At any of these meetings at any time, was there any debate about a plan to expel the Kosovo Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. It was not even mooted as an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, apart from those meetings that you attended, did you ever hear at any point General Ojdanic speak about the expulsion of Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, one more question. Did General Ojdanic do anything or say anything at any point that would indicate that he had any prejudice against the ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. As the Chief of Staff of the 1st Army, while he was the Chief of Staff and later the commander of the 1st Army, I was the chief of the security department there. There were many, dozens, of Albanian officers in the 1st Army, and they were not discriminated against in any way. They were treated the same as all the other officers of other ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you're jumping the queue, it would appear, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we're going to move in order, then I'm first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Gajic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic in this case. You've not had an opportunity to speak with me about this case at all, have you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question or two about the visit that you made to Kosovo between the 29th of May and the 7th of June of 1999, along with General Vasiljevic. You remember that visit, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get the date, the 29th --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 29th of May through the 7th of June, 1999. You went to Kosovo on an inspection visit.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct date is from the 1st to the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. During that time I want to know if you had an opportunity to inspect or conduct interviews with all of your security organs that were operating in the Kosovo theatre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We visited 16 organs in the Pristina Corps in total, including the security department in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my question was: Was that all of them or were there some that you didn't get a chance to visit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We visited in addition to the security department, as I said, the security organs, most of the security organs in the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask it this way: Do you feel that you were able to conduct a sufficiently broad investigation that you were able to provide a completely and comprehensive report to your superiors regarding the efforts that you made?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, but that was not our objective. It would have taken much more time to do all that in detail, but it was sufficient for us to get the gist of it, the general picture of the situation and to draft a good report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever get the impression from any source while you were there that there were crimes being committed that were not being properly addressed by the security organs that you were visiting and that were operating in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The picture that we got was that the security organs were doing their job quite well, that they were quite active in trying to uncover criminal offences, including war crimes but also other crimes, and that they conducted investigations and filed criminal reports. Until that time, we did not have the information about that at the security administration, but we were able to ascertain there on the site that they were actually doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the process of that investigation, did you -- did you hear about any - and I'm going to refer generally to war crimes - did you hear about any such crimes committed by persons who were not members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We had such information, but your question is not quite clear to me. But we did receive that information, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Did you or General Vasiljevic or both of you have any meeting with General Pavkovic where you explained to him the results of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- it seems to me, or rather, I'm sure on the first day when we arrived General Pavkovic knew that we were there. He came to the security department, and he said that it was good that we were there. And he asked the chief of the security department and all those present there to help us carry out the tasks that we had received from the chief of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to conclude, General, that what you found in your investigation there was almost exactly what General Pavkovic had reported in Belgrade on the meetings -- on the meetings on the 16th and the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavkovic brought the documents with him to this meeting on the 16th, and I think that this information was contained in this file, but we had broader information. He dealt with the major cases, so to speak. He didn't go into details, so he dealt with the big topics. But this -- the essence was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you even found additional matters that may be of lesser significance that were also being prosecuted and being taken care of properly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that they were of lesser importance, but those were isolated cases. For instance, we recorded a case of, let's say, Private Topalovic, who killed a civilian in Djakovica, Topalovic was put under arrest, a criminal report was filed, he was prosecuted, but we had those cases, isolated cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of an instance in early May of 1999 when General Pavkovic had come to Belgrade and made a report to superiors there about what was happening with crimes going on in Kosovo? Are you aware of that earlier visit by General Pavkovic to Belgrade? That would have been on 4 May of 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by the superiors. Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My information is that he had a meeting with President Milosevic at that time, on the 4th of May, to report matters of this nature. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the -- you talked a little bit earlier about this officer Stupar and the volunteers, and I wanted to pursue that just very briefly. It's the case, isn't it, that Stupar was located in the centre at Grocka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited that centre on the 15th of May, and Stupar was not there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if that's where he was assigned or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that question. I know that a team was set up pursuant to an order to go to that centre, but I don't recall that Stupar was on that list at that time. But as far as I can recall, that centre used to be at Bubanj Potok, and then at one point it was moved to Grocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that centre at Grocka was a reception -- a volunteer reception centre for the 1st Army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at one exhibit very quickly, it's P2594, and I want you to see paragraph 27 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is an admitted document, it's the statement of General Vasiljevic to the ICTY, to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Possibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This document is under seal, and therefore we should probably be in private session --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- In case any difficulty is caused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, I want to know where it was under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P2600 is a public version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm willing to accept either solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you able to proceed by using P2600?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it has that same paragraph 27 and probably does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to P2600 and we need the B/C/S version paragraph 27. I'm just waiting for the B/C/S version of that to come up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It appears that more than one mike is on in the courtroom and it's creating background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there's mine and the witness's, that is more than one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear English now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You'll see paragraph 27 there, and that talks about this Jugoslav Petrusic and the bypassing of appropriate procedures. And this is what General Vasiljevic said in his statement to the Prosecutor. Is that consistent with your knowledge and your understanding of that situation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did say the gist of it and that it actually jibes with what General Vasiljevic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. Let me introduce myself to you. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, and I'm one of the lawyers representing General Lazarevic. I will have a few questions for you, and as a follow-up to the last question asked by my colleague, Mr. Ackerman, I want to know when you in the security administration actually learned about the existence of this group, Pauk?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have this information that Jugoslav Petrusic was in the former Yugoslavia at an earlier stage. We had information that he had received tasks from the French intelligence service, and this indeed he confirmed in the interviews conducted with him. That sometime in 1995 he was told to deal with the Albanian factor, and from that time on he would appear from time to time in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So we did have this information, this knowledge, and the State Security Service had more knowledge because he was within their operational jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say from earlier on, that means before May 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before May, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My next question, General, is whether you can remember what position Colonel Stupar held in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really recall. He was in the General Staff or perhaps he was not in the General Staff, he was at the disposal of something or other. I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So there was a possibility that he was actually in the General Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was at a certain post -- I don't know. I really couldn't tell you. Anything that I were to tell you now would be doubtful, would be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So a moment ago you told us that people with Petrusic were sent to Kosovo and Metohija via some connections and guarantees that were proffered that they had actually gone through this procedure as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they had undergone some kind of a procedure but that was not the proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when they arrived in Kosovo to the units that they were treated or that they had the same kind of recommendations as any other volunteers that had already undergone training?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the mistake was made, the problem was somewhere in the training centre, and they were recorded as volunteers, and there was no mistake on the part of the -- any commands in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the mistake was made at the reception centre, and that is why I went there to inspect this centre. This was already discussed. A mistake was made, and that's how they managed to weasel their way there, and -- but measures were taken and they were sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have one or two more questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on. What do you mean by a mistake was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they did not undergo the kind of procedure that they had to, starting with the medical examination, a detail security background check, let me just give you those two elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I understood you to have said earlier that people were organising this for them and then guaranteeing that they had gone through the system. That's hardly a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you understood this right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, just one more question. Since they were brought in as volunteers, registered in the files, there was a mistake in the procedure but that was not known. Down there they could not have been treated as paramilitaries but as volunteers, am I not right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, just one more subject, one or two more questions. You probably know that General Vasiljevic appeared as a witness before this Court as well. He testified about the visit of General Farkas towards the end of April/beginning of May to the Pristina Corps and the inspection that he carried out at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, on transcript pages 8977 from lines 19 to 25 and page 8978, lines 1 to 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- General Vasiljevic pointed out that General Farkas praised the military security service of the Pristina Corps and the military police of the Pristina Corps and that he said that this personnel should be promoted because he saw many positive things in their work. Do you agree with this assessment and do you remember this assessment provided by General Geza Farkas?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - and I think I remember it well - he said -- it was his wording that the security organs down there were working well and the police, too, that was the formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir, my name is Dan Ivetic and I will have a few questions for you. I'll try to move as quickly as possible through them but I don't think we'll finish them today. First of all, sir, the other day when you testified on the 7th of September, you mentioned that you followed the testimony of Colonel Cucak in these proceedings. Did you also happen to follow the testimony of General Vasiljevic when he testified?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part. I had some private problems, so I did not follow it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the pause. I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. And furthermore, did you have occasion to be in communication with General Vasiljevic after his retirement from your service?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We remained in contact primarily as good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you agree that during your respective times in the service, General Vasiljevic took copious notes, for instance, of the 17th of May meeting with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did take notes. He was sitting next to me and I saw him taking notes, but what specifically -- well, he was taking notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to move to your 92 ter statement. At paragraph 166 of the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It can be brought up on the system but I was going to quote the exact language that I was asking about so that should move quicker I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You stated at that part of your statement, sir, that with regard to any plan or project regarding ethnic cleansing of the Albanians from Kosovo-Metohija: "I'm certain that such a plan or idea never existed." I want to ask you, based upon your knowledge and work and the cooperation of your service with both domestic and foreign intelligence services, am I correct that you did not possess any verified, credible, or uncontrovertible evidence linking any state organs of the FRY or Serbia with such a plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at paragraph 13 of your statement you say that a -- that your service knew of an anti-terrorist plan, action, being planned in which the army would play a significant role because activities to date, mostly through engagement of the MUP, were not very successful. I would just like to ask you to confirm if this was during the period of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the end of July onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And is it also correct that this plan that you spoke of, in addition to army units, this plan conferred assignments to units of the MUP of Serbia, based upon your information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because the MUP was, according to regulations, the main force for dealing with the terrorist forces; however, then there was an escalation and then the plan that you are referring to came into being.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, are we going to 45 after today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're only going to quarter to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Quarter to. I'm about to start a new topic that actually goes into an exhibit that I do have to cite to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as they say in all the best programmes, Mr. Gajic, that's all we've got time for today. Unfortunately, this courtroom is occupied by another case this afternoon, so we have to bring our proceedings to an end. That means that you have to return here tomorrow. Tomorrow our sitting will be at 2.15 in the afternoon. So we shall see you here again at 2.15. Meanwhile, please bear in mind what I said to you before about having no discussion with anybody about the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that you've been following it and have had some discussions, albeit not necessarily about the evidence but with at least one person who has been a witness here, it's very important that you observe that rule while you're here. So please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
